attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Matches the passage. 'This' refers to NVIDIA and other hardware sellers. It is an unqualified present-tense observation about the AI economy chain.

contract.note: The plain reading, that hardware sellers make substantial AI profits and the other layers do not, is ordinary and fair. Using calendar 2025 is reasonable. Layer-level versus company-level scope and the threshold for 'really profitable' are open questions, and the contract flags them.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 GAAP results show large profits over a period close to calendar 2025. This covers the hardware link only. It says nothing about whether the other layers lack profits.

A Gamma company release. The quoted excerpt does not actually show the profitability line, and the release gives no profit amount or basis. A small app company's self-declared profit does not show substantial profits in a whole layer.

reviews.rationale: NVIDIA's profitability is shown on a period close to 2025, but the claim's second half needs comparable AI-specific profit data showing the other layers (data center developers, hyperscalers, labs, apps) lack substantial profits. The packet has none, and hyperscaler AI profits are not broken out. Gamma's unquantified self-report neither proves nor refutes the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase of a present-tense statement that users lack assurance. The three months is the window the assurance covers, not a forecast. 'Current subscription' is slightly compressed but implied.

contract.note: Reading 'cannot with any clarity say' as the absence of reliable assurance in the standard subscription terms is an ordinary, fair proxy. If the terms allow capacity cuts at any time, users cannot say with clarity. Limiting the scope to individual subscriptions is reasonable.

evidence.note: Anthropic's consumer terms, effective Oct 2025 and so in force at publication, allow it to raise or lower capacity limits and change services at any time without notice, unless a separate agreement says otherwise. No three-month assurance.

OpenAI's terms, effective Jan 2026, allow service changes. The 30-day notice applies only to materially adverse changes to the terms. That is not a three-month guarantee that a workload stays supported.

reviews.rationale: Both providers' standard terms in force on March 31, 2026 allowed capacity and service changes within three months. Neither assured unchanged support for an existing workload. That meets the support condition. Negotiated enterprise contracts are outside scope, and the packet shows no contradicting standard assurance.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Will not save AI' is firm language, so it is a scored forecast with no deadline. The reason given about banks and insurers is context and is correctly left ungraded.

contract.note: Reading 'save AI' as averting broad economic failure of the industry fits the surrounding passage. Reading 'too big to fail' as a systemic public rescue is ordinary. The early-resolution rule is balanced.

evidence.note: NVIDIA blog, Sep 2026, showing Rubin in customer production at CoreWeave. That is deployment, not proof that Rubin rescued the industry or that the industry failed.
Punchbowl News, Oct 2026: lawmakers resist a hypothetical AI bailout. No rescue happened, and nothing shows one would or would not work.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. Neither early-resolution trigger appears in the packet: no documented rescue by Rubin or a bailout, and no conclusive industry failure settling both mechanisms. Rubin deployment and the bailout debate are only context. Not having happened yet is not failure.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Close paraphrase. 'Entire' is softened to 'the generative AI industry', and 'VCs and bankers' to 'speculation'. The core commitment, that the industry runs on unprofitable, unsustainable, speculatively funded economics, is kept.

contract.note: The ordinary reading, that the industry depends on outside financing because it cannot durably cover its full costs, is fair. Keeping current losses separate from lasting unsustainability is appropriate, and requiring industry-wide evidence matches the word 'entire'.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1, filed before the cutoff, shows an audited 2025 net loss of $42.0B, mostly fair-value changes. That is one company's loss, not industry-wide unsustainability.
MiniMax reported a 2025 adjusted (non-IFRS) loss. One company, on an adjusted basis.
Anthropic's $13B Series F in Sep 2025 shows outside financing. It does not show the services are unsustainable.
A secondhand account says Midjourney became profitable without investors. No period or figures are given, so it challenges the universal wording but is not verified for 2025.

reviews.rationale: Some large firms clearly made losses and raised outside money in 2025, which fits part of the claim. But the packet has no representative industry-wide data and nothing establishing lasting unsustainability. The Midjourney counterexample is unquantified and has no stated period. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.
